newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish shipyard workers occupy government building.
newsitem.headline: Polish shipyard workers occupy government building.

text.p: About 300 workers of the bankrupt Gdansk shipyard, the birthplace of Poland's Solidarity union, occupied the local governor's building on Monday to press their demands for the government to help to save their jobs.

They said 70 of them would stay overnight, after talks with the governor about possible credit guarantees for the yard ended inconclusively, and they warned the government there could be riots unless it took swift action.
"We are staying here until we see results. Either we will be restructured or murdered," Jerzy Borowczak, the head of the shipyard's Solidarity union, told reporters.

The northern Gdansk province's governor, Henryk Wojciechowski, told the treasury minister in a letter after meeting protesters that the state-controlled firm's 5,000 strong staff was increasingly angered by a lack of future prospects.
"The lack of a clear perspective about the future, be it liquidation or restructuring, is causing an uproar," Wojciechowski wrote.
The government, which says it is looking for strategic investors for the yard, has so far refused to extend guarantees, which banks demand before granting loans.
But Treasury Minister Miroslaw Pietrewicz said the government might still consider offering loan guarantees if the shipyard presented a viable restructuring plan.
"The government did not rule out extending credit guarantees if the shipyard presents a realistic plan which will rebuild its position," Pietrewicz told reporters in Warsaw.
He said that if the yard's receiver presented a sufficient plan on Tuesday the government could discuss the scheme as early as Wednesday.

The shipyard -- where Lech Walesa's Solidarity union was born 16 years ago in the fight against communism, went bankrupt in June after debts mounted to more than 300 million zlotys ($110 million) and banks refused it credit.
Its receiver says some $150 million in loans will be needed to continue the five best of the company's 17 outstanding contracts, enabling the yard to survive until an investor is found.
The government, dominated by an ex-communist party since 1993, says the shipyard was driven to bankruptcy by unprofitable contracts signed by its previous managements.
But critics argue the government, which has subsidised other collapsing companies, has refused to bail out the shipyard because it is a stronghold of opposition.

The shipyard has debts of 415 million zlotys ($148 million), including 127 million zlotys owed to the treasury. Since its June bankruptcy about 2,000 workers have been laid off or found other jobs and left the yard voluntarily.
